reading.body:
Nicholas Stewart is named on 8 AI lobbying filings, all filed through one firm for a single client, FDD ACTION, and naming 15 bills.

The pattern is narrow and deep. One lobbyist, one firm, one client, and a bill list that runs to fifteen separate pieces of legislation. That ratio matters: eight filings carrying fifteen bill references means the filings are dense, each one covering multiple measures rather than a single narrow ask. The disclosed prior government positions span 2011 to 2023 across congressional offices, the State Department, and the US mission to the United Nations, which is the revolving-door detail the Lobbying Disclosure Act requires filers to surface.

For AI specifically, this is the legislative layer of the stack, not the compute layer. Nothing here concerns data centers, interconnection queues, or generation. What it shows is that AI policy work is being done bill by bill, across both chambers, by a lobbyist whose disclosed background is foreign policy and national security rather than technology. That is a real signal about how AI legislation is being shaped, and it is the kind of signal that never appears in a capacity or power figure.

What the data does not tell the reader is large. It does not say what any filing asked for, whether the lobbyist's position prevailed, how much was spent, or what any of the fifteen bills would do. It does not establish that AI is the primary subject of the engagement rather than one topic among several on the same filing. It covers one lobbyist and one client, so it cannot support any claim about AI lobbying as a whole.
